tagline.text: A day in the green, blue capital where Palawan journeys begin

children.text: The gateway to Palawan and the provincial capital, and the starting point for Underground River and Honda Bay tours. A sunset walk along the Baywalk, Plaza Cuartel with its wartime history, the fenceless Iwahig Prison, a firefly river cruise, and distinctive local dishes like chaolong and tamilok fill a day or two in town on their own.

Puerto Princesa is the capital of Palawan province and the second-largest city in the Philippines by land area. The city limits span about 2,381km² — nearly four times the size of Seoul — yet the population is only around 320,000, giving it the lowest population density of any Philippine city, and just outside the center, forest, mangroves, and farmland take over. Even the famous Underground River and Honda Bay technically lie within this city's boundaries.
The city's story began on
March 4, 1872

, when Spain founded Puerto de la Princesa — "Port of the Princess" — on a deep bay along the eastern coast. During the American period came the Iwahig Penal Colony, still operating today, and World War II left behind the tragedy of Plaza Cuartel, where Japanese forces massacred American POWs. From the late 1970s, the city ran a camp for Vietnamese boat-people refugees, and the rice noodle soup they brought became today's local specialty, chaolong.

Since the 1990s, the city government has taken the lead in strictly enforcing bans on littering and smoking in public places and pushing tree-planting campaigns, earning it the nickname "the cleanest and greenest city in the Philippines." The city center around Rizal Avenue is close to the airport and compact enough to explore on foot, so you can drop your bags and head straight out to the cathedral, the plaza, and the seaside promenade.

Most travelers only pass through this city on the way to El Nido or Port Barton, but setting aside a day of your own lets you see Palawan's history, food, and daily life up close. It suits travelers staying before or after an Underground River or Honda Bay tour, families, and anyone who likes a city's flavor and stories more than its beaches.

blocks.title: Sunset and street-food seafood at the Baywalk

children.text: A seaside promenade running along Puerto Princesa Bay, where locals gather at sunset to stroll and exercise. In the evening, stalls selling grilled skewers and seafood line up, making it an easy spot for a light meal.
The site of the Palawan Massacre, where on
December 14, 1944
Japanese forces herded about 140 American POWs into an air-raid shelter and set it on fire. Today it's a quiet garden with the old barracks walls and a memorial, and admission is free.
Right next to Plaza Cuartel, this Gothic-style cathedral with striking spires was completed in its current form in the early 1960s. From the plaza in front, you can see the sea beyond the bay.
Built in
under American rule, this "prison without bars" has inmates living and working on a sprawling farm. There's a souvenir shop selling woodcarvings and bags made by inmates, about
30–40 minutes
by car from the city center.
After dark, ride a small boat up the mangrove-lined river and watch fireflies blink on every tree like a Christmas display. The clearer and moonless the night, the more vivid it is.

Buy the local specialty hopia and "Spec roll" at Baker's Hill, a bakery-garden on a hill west of the city, then head up to nearby Mitra's Ranch for a view over Honda Bay, plus horseback riding and a zipline.

At the Palawan Wildlife Rescue and Conservation Center you can see endangered Philippine and saltwater crocodiles, and the butterfly garden shows off Palawan's butterflies alongside models of indigenous Palawan life — a good stop for a family trip with kids.
A small museum in the old city hall building next to Mendoza Park, displaying artifacts from Tabon Caves and indigenous crafts.

The firefly cruise and Honda Bay tour are easily cancelled by rain, so in the rainy season it's best to put them earlier in your itinerary rather than on the last day, leaving room to reschedule.

1 hour 20 minutes

Passenger ferries to the Cuyo Islands and other Sulu Sea islands also depart from Puerto Princesa's port.

November
through
May
is the dry season and the best time to visit, especially
January–April
, when rain is scarce and the sea is calm, so Underground River and Honda Bay tours are less likely to be canceled. Midday temperatures run around
, so it's best to pack city sightseeing into the morning and evening and rest indoors at a museum or restaurant during the hottest hours.
From
June
to
October

, the southwest monsoon brings frequent showers, and the firefly cruise is sometimes canceled on rainy nights. Palawan sees fewer direct typhoon hits than central Philippines, but there are still days when the sea route is blocked by the storm's outer bands. Around the city's founding anniversary on
March 4
, the Balayong Festival brings a street parade and the planting of balayong trees, and in
June
, Baragatan, the province-wide cultural festival, runs for about three weeks.

Accommodation clusters along Rizal Avenue, which runs from the airport to the cathedral, and its surroundings, close to restaurants, money changers, and travel agencies. A guesthouse runs about
per night, and a mid-range hotel with a pool about

. The city sits inside the bay, so there's almost nowhere to swim in the sea; if you want to swim, take a Honda Bay tour or choose a beach resort on the outskirts. Underground River tours pick up before dawn, so staying within the pickup area is convenient.

The must-try dish is chaolong, a local take on the rice noodle soup brought by Vietnamese refugees. Rice noodles, bean sprouts, and herbs go into a beef or pork broth, served with baguette, and a bowl costs around

— popular as breakfast. Tamilok, a shipworm that lives inside mangrove wood, is a Palawan specialty eaten raw, dipped in vinegar and lime; you can try it alongside crocodile sisig at Kinabuchs Grill and Bar on Rizal Avenue. Ka Lui, decorated in bamboo and wood, is an old, shoes-off seafood restaurant with great atmosphere. Popular souvenirs include Palawan-grown cashew nuts and Baker's Hill hopia.
Underground River permits are limited in number, so book your date through a travel agency before arriving in Puerto Princesa, then plan the rest of your city itinerary around it.
Most city sights are close together, so it's efficient to walk to the cathedral, Plaza Cuartel, and the museum in the morning, then tour the outlying sights by tricycle in the afternoon.
Shared and chartered tricycle fares differ a lot, so settle which one you're taking and the fare before you get in.
The Palawan Museum is often closed on Sundays, and the crocodile farm may keep shorter weekend hours, so it's worth checking before you visit.
The firefly cruise is more impressive around the new moon than the full moon, and photos rarely turn out well, so it's better enjoyed with your own eyes.
El Nido and Port Barton have few ATMs and high fees, so it's best to withdraw plenty of cash in Puerto Princesa before heading out.
Grab is unavailable or has few cars here, so it's safer to book airport pickups or early-morning rides through your accommodation in advance.
Cashew nuts are cheaper at city souvenir shops and markets than at the airport, so buy them the day before you leave.
You can go on your own instead of joining an agency tour. The Iwahig firefly pier is at kilometer 20 of the southern national highway, about
35 minutes
by car from the city, and from
6 PM
you can take a boat (3 people) for
. Check the latest fares in the
Puerto Princesa City Tourism Office
notices.
Ka Lui is closed on Sundays and opens only for lunch (
11 AM–2 PM
) and dinner (
); seats fill up quickly in the evening, so it's best to reserve by phone before you go.

Puerto Princesa strictly enforces ordinances against smoking and littering in public places, and violators pay a fine. Even vaping is allowed only in designated areas, so it's worth checking the latest rules.
Iwahig Penal Colony is an actual, operating correctional facility. Get permission before photographing inmates, and don't enter restricted areas.
Plaza Cuartel is a memorial site, so it's proper etiquette to avoid rowdy behavior or climbing on the monument for photos.
Mosquitoes are plentiful around the mangroves at sunset and on the firefly tour, so wear long sleeves and bring repellent.
The midday heat is intense, causing frequent dehydration and heatstroke. Bring water and a hat, and rest indoors in the early afternoon.
The city center is relatively safe, but watch for pickpockets in crowded spots like the Baywalk or market, and avoid quiet streets late at night.
